In the Hinsberg’s test, an amine is reacted with benzene sulfonyl chloride. If a product forms, the amine is either a primary or secondary amine because tertiary amines can not form sulfonamides. Hinsberg’s test is used to distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary amines. The Hinsberg’s reagent is a solution of aqueous sodium hydroxide and benzene sulfonyl chloride. Procedure

Add 4-5 mL of an amine to a large test tube. Add 5 mL of benzene sulfonyl chloride and 10 mL of 10% NaOH and shake vigorously to mix. If yes, it is tertiary but if it is insoluble, then secondary amine is present.

v. 2-chloro-3,3-dimethylpentan-2-amine

Project

Hinsberg’s test is used to distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary amines. The Hinsberg’s reagent is a solution of aqueous sodium hydroxide and benzene sulfonyl chloride. In the Hinsberg’s test, an amine is reacted with benzene sulfonyl chloride. If a product forms, the amine is either a primary or secondary amine because tertiary amines can not form sulfonamides. If the sulfonamide that forms dissolves in aqueous sodium hydroxide solution, it is a primary amine. If the sulfonamide is insoluble in aqueous sodium hydroxide, it is a secondary amine. The sulfonamide of a primary amine is soluble in an aqueous base because it still possesses an acidic hydrogen on the nitrogen, which can be lost to form a sodium salt.

Procedure

Add 4-5 mL of an amine to a large test tube. Add 5 mL of benzene sulfonyl chloride and 10 mL of 10% NaOH and shake vigorously to mix. Check for the presence of a single layer (primary amine) or a double layer (secondary amine) in the solution. If there is a double layer, draw off the lower aqueous layer with a separating funnel and check if the organic layer is soluble in 5% HCl. If yes, it is tertiary but if it is insoluble, then secondary amine is present.
